lead: Real control elements do not keep a fixed gain for every input. A valve stops opening past its travel limit, a motor does not move until the drive overcomes friction, and a gear train loses motion in the gap between teeth. Saturation and dead zone are static nonlinearities y=f(x): the output at an instant depends only on the input at that instant. Backlash is a nonlinearity with memory: its output depends on direction and history, so one input can give two outputs. Three shapes cover many such cases: saturation, dead zone and backlash. They explain why a loop that is stable for small signals can show error, slow response or a steady oscillation.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 block diagrams and Unit 5 on-off control; this chapter does not repeat them.

blocks.text: Static nonlinearity. A linear block obeys y=Gx for all x. A static nonlinearity obeys y=f(x): f is a fixed curve, not a differential equation. The output has no memory of past inputs. Real valves, amplifiers, sensors and gears are linear only over a range. Outside that range the curve bends; the loop behaves differently for large signals.
y = kx for |x| ≤ a; y = M for x > a; y = −M for x < −a; M = k a
blocks.where: x is input; y is output; k is the linear gain; a is the input saturation threshold; M is the output limit. Some syllabi call this a limiter or clipping.

blocks.text: Saturation means the element cannot deliver more than M. Below a, the slope is k. Above a, the slope is zero, so the incremental gain falls. In a closed loop, small errors see full gain, but a large error cannot push harder. The loop may look fast for small steps and slow for large steps. A controller with integral action may keep integrating while the actuator is stuck at M; that is integrator windup, and it needs anti-windup logic.

items: A 4–20 mA transmitter clips near 20 mA.
An op-amp output clips at its supply rail.
A valve stops at fully open or fully closed.

blocks.text: A dead zone is a flat interval around zero. The element produces no output until the input is large enough to overcome it.
y = 0 for |x| < δ; y = k(x − δ) for x ≥ δ; y = k(x + δ) for x ≤ −δ
blocks.where: δ is the dead-zone half-width; k is the slope outside the dead zone. Some syllabi call this a deadband.

blocks.text: Inside |x|<δ, the slope is zero. Outside, the slope is k but the curve is shifted. A small sine input may produce no output, or a distorted output. In a feedback loop, a small error gives no corrective action, so the error can stay. This is a common cause of steady-state error in valves with stiction or in sensors with a deadband. The effect is worst when the dead zone is comparable with the required accuracy.
Backlash is a gap between two moving parts. The input must move through the gap before the output moves. The output therefore depends on direction and on where the input has been.
At a reversal, y stays at its last value until x has moved 2b; then y = x − b when x increases; y = x + b when x decreases
blocks.where: b is the half-gap; the total gap is 2b. Some syllabi call this play or lash.

blocks.text: At a reversal, the output does not follow immediately. This memory makes backlash a multi-valued relation: one x can give two y values. In a loop, backlash causes lost motion. The controller pushes, the output lags, then catches up and overshoots. Repeated reversals can produce hunting or a limit cycle. A gear train, a leadscrew nut and a loose linkage all show backlash. Describing-function analysis (see 7.2) uses these shapes to predict oscillation; limit cycles are treated in 7.4.

figure.caption: Saturation flattens at ±10 mA after ±2 mA; dead zone is zero between ±0.2 mA; backlash traces a loop of width 0.2 mA.

spec.aria: The saturation curve flattens at plus and minus 10, the dead zone is flat between plus and minus 0.2, and the backlash curve traces a loop of width 0.2.

examples.question: Three separate elements have: saturation M=10 mA, a=2 mA, k=5; dead zone δ=0.2 mA, k=5; backlash b=0.1 mA. For x=3 mA, find each output; backlash input increases from 0.
steps: Saturation: compare x=3 mA with a=2 mA. Since 3 > 2, the output is clamped at the limit M. So y=10 mA.
Dead zone: compare x=3 mA with δ=0.2 mA. Since 3 > 0.2, use y=k(x−δ)=5(3−0.2) mA = 5×2.8 mA = 14 mA.
Backlash: the input is increasing from 0, so use y=x−b=(3−0.1) mA = 2.9 mA.
examples.answer: Saturation gives 10 mA, dead zone gives 14 mA, and backlash gives 2.9 mA.
examples.check:
M = 10.0
a = 2.0
k = 5.0
delta = 0.2
b = 0.1
x = 3.0
sat = M if x > a else (k*x if x >= -a else -M)
dead = 0.0 if abs(x) < delta else (k*(x-delta) if x > delta else k*(x+delta))
backlash = x - b
print(f'{sat:g}')
print(f'{dead:g}')
print(f'{backlash:g}')

traps: Backlash is not a single curve: the same x can give two outputs. You must state direction and starting point.
Saturation threshold a is an input value; M is the output limit. M=ka holds only when the linear segment reaches the limit.
Dead zone and saturation both create flat parts, but dead zone is near zero and removes small signals; saturation is far from zero and limits large signals.
At the boundary |x|=a or |x|=δ, both pieces of the equation must give the same value; a mismatch means the piecewise rule is wrong.

quiz.a: The output depends only on the present input, not on past inputs; the relation is a fixed curve.

quiz.q: Why does saturation lower the effective gain for large signals?
quiz.a: Beyond a the slope is zero, so the incremental output change per input change falls to zero.

quiz.q: A dead zone has δ=0.2 mA and k=5. For x=−3 mA, find y.
A backlash element has b=0.1 mA. The input increases from 0 to 3 mA. Find y.
quiz.a: On the increasing branch, y=x−b=(3−0.1) mA=2.9 mA.

quiz.q: Why can a dead zone cause steady-state error in a feedback loop?
quiz.a: A small error gives no corrective output, so the plant stays where it is until the error exceeds δ.

quiz.q: How does backlash lead to hunting?
quiz.a: At each reversal the output waits through the gap; the loop then overshoots, reverses, and repeats the lost motion.

quiz.q: Give alternative names for the three nonlinearities.
quiz.a: Saturation: limiter or clipping; dead zone: deadband; backlash: play or lash.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, backlash models are used in robot joints and gearboxes, dead-zone models in hydraulic valves, and saturation models in motor drives and power converters. Anti-windup design and actuator limit handling are standard in PLC and drone flight-control code. Research extends these shapes to friction, hysteresis and smart actuators. Search terms: backlash compensation, dead-zone inverse, actuator saturation, anti-windup.
